summary.text: Feudalism was a mix of customs and systems that flourished in medieval Europe from the 9th to 15th centuries, built around land held in exchange for service or labour.
In its classic definition it was a set of reciprocal legal and military obligations of the warrior nobility, centred on lords, vassals, and fiefs.
A broader definition also covers the clergy and the peasantry, who were bound by a system of manorialism, so that all three estates of the realm are included.

items.prompt: A ruler has cavalry to support but no bureaucracy to pay for it. If this follows the Carolingian pattern, what does the ruler end up doing?

options.label: Sending the horsemen home to rely on infantry
Hiring foreign soldiers with imported goods
Taxing peasants to fill a standing treasury
Giving land to the mounted soldiers

items.explain: The Carolingian Empire lacked the bureaucratic infrastructure to support cavalry without allocating land to its mounted troops.

items.prompt: Mounted soldiers in a breaking-up empire begin to pass down the land they were given. What does this do to the empire's central power?

options.label: Their power stays limited to war and never reaches daily life
Their power spreads into many areas and weakens central rule
Their power is taken back by the ruler in each generation
Their power fades quickly because heirs cannot hold the land

items.explain: Mounted soldiers secured hereditary rule over their land, and their power came to cover social, political, judicial and economic matters, which significantly diminished unitary power.

paragraphs.heading: A bargain over land
paragraphs.text: Feudalism, or the feudal system, was not one neat scheme but a mix of customs and arrangements that thrived in medieval Europe between the 9th and 15th centuries. At its heart was a trade: you held land, and in return you owed service or labour. A grant of land given in exchange for service was first called a beneficium in Latin documents, and later a feudum, or fief. The classic definition, from the historian François Louis Ganshof in 1944, looks only at the warrior nobility and their two-way legal and military duties, built around lords, vassals and fiefs.

paragraphs.heading: A wider view
paragraphs.text: Marc Bloch's 1939 book Feudal Society cast the net wider. It takes in the duties of every one of the three estates: nobles, clergy, and those who lived off their labour, above all the peasants, who were bound by manorialism. This whole order is often called a feudal society, after Bloch. Ganshof himself said his own account dealt only with the narrow, technical, legal meaning of the word.

paragraphs.heading: How it grew
paragraphs.text: Feudalism usually took root where an empire came apart. One example is the Carolingian Empire of the 9th century, which lacked the bureaucracy needed to support cavalry without handing land to those mounted troops. Over time the horsemen made their hold on that land hereditary, and their power over it spread into social, political, judicial and economic life. These new powers sharply weakened the central authority of such empires.

paragraphs.heading: From cattle to land
paragraphs.text: The word feudal comes from medieval Latin feudālis, built on feudum, 'fee', first recorded in a charter of Charles the Fat in 884. One theory, put forward by Johan Hendrik Caspar Kern in 1870, links it to a Frankish word joining 'cattle' and 'goods', meaning a movable thing of value. Bloch explains that by the early 10th century land was priced in money but often paid for in goods such as weapons, clothes, horses or food, a practice called feos. The term was later used for land handed over in return for loyalty, so a word for movable property came to mean landed property.

paragraphs.heading: A name given later
paragraphs.text: People in the Middle Ages did not see feudalism as a formal political system, even though the word grows out of the Latin they used. The adjective feudal was in use by 1406, and French legal writing used 'féodal' in 1614. In The Wealth of Nations (1776), Adam Smith, trying to describe economic systems, effectively coined 'feudal government' and 'feudal system'. John Whitaker brought in the word 'feudalism' itself, along with the idea of a feudal pyramid, in The History of Manchester in 1771.

paragraphs.heading: Is it a useful idea
paragraphs.text: Ever since Elizabeth A. Brown's 'The Tyranny of a Construct' in 1974 and Fiefs and Vassals by Susan Reynolds in 1994, medieval historians have argued, without reaching an answer, whether feudalism helps us understand the Middle Ages at all. Some say the word has been used in so many ways that it has lost any specific meaning. Others stretch it beyond Europe, most often to Japan under the shoguns, and sometimes to ancient Egypt or China's Spring and Autumn period. Even within Europe, scholars find that Poland and Lithuania resembled the Western pattern in some ways but not all.
